name: Skills
tagline: A curated box of 27 agent skills for Claude Code - from test-driven development to debugging to architecture reviews.
sentence: Install Matt Pocock's skills collection and your Claude Code agent gets 27 new abilities: /tdd writes tests first, /caveman debugs with print statements, /todoist turns a task into a checklist, and 24 more - each one a focused behavior the agent follows exactly.
replaces: Writing custom CLAUDE.md rules for each workflow you want the agent to follow

visual.alt: The skills.sh website showing a grid of available skills from the mattpocock/skills collection, each with a name, description and install count.
visual.caption: The skills.sh catalog showing Matt Pocock's skill collection: 27 skills, each with a short description of what it teaches the agent.

board.say: Your AI coding agent is powerful but generic. It doesn't know your team's workflow - whether you want tests first, how you debug, or how you hand off work.
board.eg: You want Claude Code to always write the test before the code, but every time you forget to say so, it writes the code first.

board.say: You install the skills collection - one command - and start using the new slash commands.
board.eg: `npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills` installs all 27 skills. Or pick one: `npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/tdd`.

board.say: A slash command followed by your normal prompt.
board.eg: `/tdd Add a retry mechanism to the API client` - the agent writes a failing test first, then makes it pass.

board.say: Each skill injects a specific workflow into the agent's thinking. The agent follows that workflow instead of its default behavior.
steps: /tdd: writes a failing test, then writes the code to make it pass, then refactors
/caveman: debugs with print statements instead of reasoning about the bug - forces the agent to observe before concluding
/todoist: breaks a task into a checkbox list and works through it step by step
18 user-invoked skills and 9 that activate automatically based on what you're doing
board.eg: Deepak Bagada (CEO, SaaSNext) installed the collection across 5 engineering teams: /tdd eliminated missing test suites, /diagnose cut debugging time roughly in half, handoff docs cut task resumption from 90 minutes to 15.

board.say: An agent that follows your team's workflows instead of guessing what you want.

outputs.eg: Every task follows the same pattern - tests first, debugging by observation, clear handoff documentation
One test showed 62% fewer tokens (the units AI charges are measured in) in debugging sessions using /caveman
20-40% faster time to a correct pull request in one week-long test

before: Your agent improvises a workflow each time. Sometimes it writes tests first, sometimes it doesn't. Debugging is a guessing game.
You write custom CLAUDE.md rules for each behavior you want, and they're hard to share across projects or teams.
after: 27 pre-built workflows you can invoke by name. /tdd for test-first, /caveman for print-debugging, /todoist for checklists.
Skills are shareable packages: install once, use across every project.
uses_note: Skills has 274K stars. Two named uses found with measurable outcomes.

uses.what: Installed the skills collection across 5 engineering teams and adapted 12 of 27 skills for production TypeScript projects. Results: TDD adoption eliminated missing test suites, debugging time cut roughly in half with /diagnose, handoff docs cut task resumption from 90 minutes to 15.
Tested skills on an Astro/TypeScript project for one week. /caveman debugging reduced output tokens by 62%, time-to-correct-PR down 20-40%. (Note: andrew.ooo is AI-agent-operated, human-supervised.)

coverage.meta: Mixed review: /grill-with-docs and /caveman effective, /tdd less useful for complex UI

steps: Install all 27 skills: `npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills`. Or try one: `npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills/tdd`.
Try `/tdd Add a retry mechanism to the API client` and watch the agent write a failing test first, then make it pass.
Try `/caveman` on a bug you're stuck on - the agent debugs by adding print statements and observing the output instead of guessing.
try.paste:
/skillspector https://github.com/mattpocock/skills

If that scan passes: install the collection, run /tdd on a simple feature, then /caveman on a known bug. Report whether the agent followed the skill's workflow and what the result looked like. 10 minutes max.

footprint.disk: Lightweight - skills are Markdown instruction files, not heavy packages.
footprint.memory: No measurable overhead. Skills are context instructions, not running processes.
footprint.runs_on: Claude Code, Codex, or any agent that supports skills. Needs Node.js for the installer.

best_for: You use Claude Code daily and want consistent, named workflows - test-first, print-debugging, task checklists - without writing custom rules
You lead a team and want everyone's agent to follow the same practices
skip_if: You don't use Claude Code or a compatible AI agent - the skills need a host
You prefer writing your own custom rules and want full control over every prompt

alternatives.name: ECC (Everything Claude Code)
alternatives.line: 261 skills and 63 sub-agents - much larger collection but also a bigger commitment. Skills focuses on 27 high-quality, focused workflows.

alternatives.name: Custom CLAUDE.md rules
alternatives.line: Write your own rules in CLAUDE.md. More work, but fully customized to your project. Skills saves that time with pre-built, tested workflows.

watch: **Made by Matt Pocock, known for TypeScript education.** This is a personal project, not a company product. He maintains it actively, but it depends on one person.
**Not all skills are equally useful.** The DevTalk review found /tdd less useful for complex UI work, while /grill-with-docs and /caveman were strong.
**The andrew.ooo review was AI-agent-operated.** The 62% token reduction number comes from a blog that is human-supervised but AI-written - weight it accordingly.
**Skills are Markdown files.** They work by injecting instructions into the agent's context. No sandboxing, no isolation - they change how the agent thinks, which is the point but also the risk.
